reference.source: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders / IUIS classification of inborn errors of immunity
clinicalPearls: The acronym captures the tetrad of warts, hypogammaglobulinaemia, recurrent infections and myelokathexis, though not every feature is present in each patient
Peripheral blood shows profound neutropenia despite a hypercellular bone marrow densely packed with mature, degenerating neutrophils held back from release (myelokathexis)
Human papillomavirus disease is characteristic and severe, with extensive cutaneous and anogenital warts and a raised risk of HPV-driven malignancy
Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infection reflects both neutropenia and impaired humoral immunity with low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine responses
Lymphopenia affecting B and T cells is usual, and the neutropenia paradoxically worsens the picture despite abundant marrow reserve
Neutrophil counts often rise transiently during acute infection or after corticosteroid stress, a clue to marrow retention rather than production failure
Most cases arise from autosomal dominant gain-of-function truncating variants in CXCR4 that prevent normal receptor internalisation
A CXCR4 antagonist (plerixafor) mobilises retained marrow neutrophils and lymphocytes into the circulation and can reduce infection and wart burden
reference.pathophysiology: WHIM syndrome is caused by gain-of-function variants, usually truncations of the C-terminal tail of the chemokine receptor CXCR4, that impair receptor desensitisation and internalisation after binding its ligand CXCL12. The resulting exaggerated and sustained CXCR4 signalling anchors mature neutrophils and lymphocytes within the bone marrow, preventing their egress into the blood despite adequate production; the retained neutrophils age and die in the marrow, producing myelokathexis. Persistent peripheral neutropenia and lymphopenia, together with impaired antibody production, underlie the recurrent bacterial infections, while defective trafficking and immunity permit uncontrolled human papillomavirus infection.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and differential demonstrating persistent neutropenia and lymphopenia
Bone marrow examination showing hypercellularity with myelokathexis and degenerating mature neutrophils
Serum immunoglobulins with hypogammaglobulinaemia and specific antibody responses to vaccines
CXCR4 gene sequencing for gain-of-function variants
HPV assessment including cervical and anogenital surveillance
redFlags: New or rapidly changing anogenital or cutaneous lesion suggesting HPV-driven malignancy
Overwhelming bacterial infection in the setting of severe neutropenia
Progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent pneumonia and bronchiectasis
Cytopenias or marrow changes raising concern for evolving haematological disease
reference.prognosis: With immunoglobulin replacement, infection prophylaxis and measures to raise the neutrophil count, many patients survive into adulthood, but the persistent HPV burden carries a significant long-term risk of malignancy and chronic morbidity from bronchiectasis.
pitfalls: Interpreting the neutropenia as a production defect and overlooking the hypercellular marrow of myelokathexis
Missing the diagnosis when only some components of the tetrad are present
Neglecting systematic HPV surveillance and vaccination in affected patients
Attributing recurrent infection solely to neutropenia and failing to detect the antibody deficiency
Being reassured by transient rises in neutrophil count during acute illness
